   record(store, admin.id, 'account.interest-rate', accountId)
   return updated
 }
+
+/** Freeze the user's own account: it takes no transfers until an administrator unfreezes it. */
+export function freezeAccount(store, user, id) {
+  const account = getOwnAccount(store, user, id)
+  if (account.frozenAt) throw new HttpError(409, 'already frozen')
+  const frozen = store.update('accounts', id, { frozenAt: now(), updatedAt: now() })
+  record(store, user.id, 'account.freeze', id)
+  return frozen
+}
+
+/** Unfreeze an account. Administrators only. */
+export function unfreezeAccount(store, admin, id) {
+  const account = store.get('accounts', id)
+  if (!account) throw new HttpError(404, 'no such account')
+  if (!account.frozenAt) throw new HttpError(409, 'not frozen')
+  const thawed = store.update('accounts', id, { frozenAt: null, updatedAt: now() })
+  record(store, admin.id, 'account.unfreeze', id)
+  return thawed
+}

findings.short_summary: Freeze webhook fires before ownership check
findings.summary: POST /accounts/:id/freeze calls notify('account.freeze-requested', ...) before freezeAccount() performs its ownership and existence checks and before store.save(), so the card-processor webhook fires for requests that are then rejected — and can fire for a freeze that is never durably saved.
findings.failure_scenario: Empirically reproduced with a stub webhook endpoint: member Cy, who owns no account, calls POST /accounts/<Bob's account id>/freeze and POST /accounts/does-not-exist/freeze. Both return 404 {error:'no such account'} and no account's frozenAt is ever set, yet in both cases the server had already sent account.freeze-requested with {accountId, requestedBy: Cy's id}. Every other notifying route in server.js (account.closed, transfer.created, deposit.created) notifies only after store.save() succeeds; freeze is the only one that inverts the order. notify() is fire-and-forget with no cancellation, so the external processor acts on an unauthorized request.

findings.short_summary: publicAccount omits frozen state from all responses

findings.failure_scenario: An admin calls POST /accounts/:id/unfreeze after a member froze the account. The call returns 200 and frozenAt is cleared, and transfers are immediately allowed again (transfers.js:22), but no webhook of any kind is sent. An external card processor that blocked the card on account.freeze-requested is never told to unblock it, and there is no event, retry, or reconciliation path that would ever correct the divergence.

findings.summary: accrueInterest() skips only accounts with closedAt set and never checks frozenAt, so the daily interest job keeps crediting a frozen account's balance — the same 'no movement while frozen' guarantee the transfer guard enforces, unenforced on the scheduled path.
findings.failure_scenario: accrueInterest(store) credits interest to an account whose frozenAt is set, growing its balance while the account is frozen. Reproduced with a $10,000 balance at 20% APR yielding +547 cents on a frozen account in a single run.

findings.summary: freezeAccount() never checks account.closedAt (unlike setInterestRate(), which does at accounts.js:62) and closeAccount() never checks account.frozenAt, so a closed account can be frozen and — more seriously — an owner can close an account out from under an active freeze, routing around the administrator-only unfreeze control the feature is built on.
findings.short_summary: freeze and close ignore each other's state
findings.failure_scenario: An owner freezes an account, then calls POST /accounts/:id/close; closeAccount ignores frozenAt and succeeds, so the owner has unilaterally changed the state of a frozen account without the admin whose approval the design requires. In the other direction, an already-closed account can be frozen, and an admin can then successfully unfreeze that closed account, clearing frozenAt with no gate on closedAt anywhere in the freeze/unfreeze path.

**Status: complete** — no agents died, nothing was cut by the ceiling, and the project's own `npm run check && npm test` passed clean on the head commit before any angle ran. Result JSON written to `calibration/results/0.4.0/branch-origin-feat-freeze-account.json`.

Six root causes, all six upheld. Findings are in the panel above.

**Budget** — used 19 of a computed ceiling of 20 (you passed no `--agents`, so the script took the smallest ceiling with room for every fixed angle plus two of the scout's): 1 scout, 6 finders, 1 triage, 10 skeptics, 1 critic. No retries, no same-site check needed (triage left no two groups at one site; `merged: 0`). 14 raw findings collapsed to 6 root causes — the webhook-ordering defect alone was found independently by five of the six angles.

**Angles** — six run, all fixed: authz-and-attribution, silent-drops, boundary-contract, tests-that-dont-test, correctness, data-integrity. The scout dropped two with reasons: *migrations-and-rollout* (004 is shaped identically to 002/003, purely additive, and every consumer treats `undefined` and `null` alike) and *security* (no new injection/secret/CORS surface; the one new disclosure risk is the same mechanism as the authz finding). No project angles — `.claude/adv-review.json` defines only `checks` and `isolate`.

**Verification** — 0 refuted, 0 unverified, 0 dismissed for doubt alone. But all six were **upheld only after a skeptic corrected them** — severity or summary was wrong as first reported in every case — so read the summaries as the skeptics' version, not the finders'. Three of the four critical/high root causes got a full three-lens panel (3 of 3 skeptics failed to refute each); the fourth (`unfreeze` sends no webhook) and the two mediums were each verified by a single skeptic. Nothing was downgraded, and nothing is pre-existing — every defect arrives with this branch.

**What the critic says the angles missed** — none of this survived a refutation attempt, so check it by hand:

1. **The diff breaks the project's own written policy.** `docs/security.md:8-9` requires authorisation "before any write, any file, any log line about the resource, and any webhook", and that file's preamble says a change that deliberately breaks a rule must amend it in the same PR. This diff does neither. `README.md:54` is also now stale — it still says webhooks fire "after the response", which the freeze route no longer does.
2. **No test exercises the freeze webhook at all.** The one test that configures a real `webhook.url` and asserts the fired-event list (`test/server.test.js:79`, line 104) was not extended. The new freeze test calls `serve(store, dir)` with no webhook option, so `notify()` takes its no-op branch — which is exactly why 35/35 tests pass over a critical defect.
3. **The feature's safety rests on best-effort delivery.** `webhooks.js` is untouched: two retries over ~6s, then a `console.warn` nobody reads, and no field on the account or in the audit log recording whether the processor was ever told. A frozen account whose webhook ultimately failed is indistinguishable from one that succeeded.

**Cleanup** — all 19 worktrees and their branches removed; your checkout is untouched, still `main` @ `7fc1c3c`, clean, with `git worktree list` back to one entry.

Nothing to post: this is a branch with no PR, so there is no comment target — `--no-post` and the review ends here.
